items.prompt: Which part of recovery after a crunch usually resolves first?
choices: Sleep and the adrenaline coming down
Trust between the people involved
Belief that urgent still means urgent
items.explanation: A quick reset happens with rest alone, within days.

items.prompt: What does acute recovery mean?
choices: The slow rebuilding of lost team trust
The short reset once the crisis stops
A formal program run by the company
items.explanation: It covers sleep and adrenaline, and it is fast.

items.prompt: What does capacity rebuilding restore?
choices: Only the hours of lost sleep
The original incident timeline
Trust, confidence and slack
items.explanation: It repairs what the period spent beyond tiredness.

items.prompt: Which clock runs in days?
choices: Acute recovery
Capacity rebuilding
Neither of the two
items.explanation: Acute recovery is quick; rebuilding takes weeks to months.

items.prompt: The runner feels normal by Wednesday. What does that feeling mostly measure?
choices: Whether the tendons are rebuilt
The fast layer, such as soreness
Whether the training base is back
items.explanation: Soreness is the part you can feel, so it is the part you notice.

items.prompt: Why can a team look recovered a week after a crunch?
choices: Everything has been fully repaired
Slow costs never apply to teams
The fast layer settles quickly
items.explanation: Rested people look fine while slower costs remain.

items.prompt: When the incidents stop, what has ended?
choices: The acute event only
All the cost of the period
The need for any follow-up
items.explanation: The event ends; its cost does not end with it.

items.prompt: Does capacity rebuild by itself once pressure lifts?
choices: Yes, within a single weekend
No, it needs deliberate work
Yes, as soon as the alerts stop
items.explanation: Time alone repairs sleep, not trust or slack.

items.prompt: A team's last incident closed on Friday. By Wednesday everyone is rested and joking again. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The team has recovered in full, since morale is visibly high
The fast layer has recovered; the slow layer is still unknown
The team is hiding a problem, since cheerfulness is suspicious
Nothing can be concluded because recovery cannot be assessed
items.explanation: Feeling rested measures acute recovery. Trust, slack and the meaning of urgent are not visible in the same way, so they stay unknown, not good and not bad.
items.reference:
Two clocks

Acute recovery

Days: sleep, adrenaline

Capacity rebuilding

Weeks to months: trust, slack
Why: the crisis ending only starts the fast clock; the slow clock needs deliberate work.
items.learnMore:
Feeling recovered versus being recovered

The layer you can feel recovers first, which makes it a poor signal for the layer you cannot.

Common mistake

Reading a rested, cheerful team as a repaired one.
items.reflection: Think of a hard stretch you came through. What felt normal quickly, and what took much longer to feel normal?

items.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts the two recovery layers?
choices: Sleep returns alone; trust and slack need deliberate repair
Both layers return by themselves, though at slightly different speeds over time
Trust returns by itself, while sleep needs a formal program to be restored
Neither layer returns without a manager scheduling something specific for it
items.explanation: Passive time repairs the fast layer. The slow layer is spent, not just tired, so it has to be rebuilt on purpose.

Fast layer within days, slow layer over weeks or months

items.prompt: What does carrying it forward mean?
choices: Handing the same project over to the next team
Old cost resurfacing later, unrelated-looking
Writing the lessons into the team wiki
items.explanation: Unpaid cost reappears in disguise, so the link is lost.

items.prompt: Where does unresolved crunch cost usually go?
choices: It vanishes once the weekend has passed
It is absorbed fully by the system
It resurfaces later in a different form
items.explanation: It does not disappear; it shows up looking unrelated.

items.prompt: Which is a sign of carried-forward cost?
choices: A small alert triggering a full scramble
A cleanly closed and filed incident postmortem
A planned and well-attended retro
items.explanation: Overreaction to a minor event can trace to an old crunch.

items.prompt: What does a recovery practice sit between?
choices: Two unrelated sprints on the shared calendar
The crisis ending and business as usual
The hiring plan and the budget cycle
items.explanation: It is the deliberate step after the crisis ends.

items.prompt: Is the crunch itself always the failure?
choices: Yes, every crunch is a management failure
Yes, unless it is under two weeks long
No, the missing close-out is the failure
items.explanation: Some crunches are unavoidable; leaving them unclosed is not.

items.prompt: Why is the runner's stress injury blamed on shoes?
choices: The cause is weeks old and not obviously linked
Shoes are always the main cause of running injury
The runner never checked their shoes at all
items.explanation: A delayed effect hides its real source.

items.prompt: What does a named debrief do?
choices: Replaces the need for any rest
Closes the period on purpose
Assigns blame for each incident
items.explanation: It marks the period as hard and starts repair.

items.prompt: What happens if the calendar simply resumes?
choices: The slow layer repairs itself quickly
The fast layer fails to recover too
The slow layer goes unrepaired
items.explanation: Nobody pays the slower cost, so it waits to reappear.

items.prompt: Three months after a brutal quarter, a quiet teammate resigns saying it 'just wasn't the right fit'. Which reading best fits this unit?
choices: It is certainly caused by the quarter, since resignations never have other causes
It is certainly unrelated, since three months is too long to matter
An unrelated move, or cost from the unclosed quarter surfacing late
It shows the team needed more pay, which settles the question
items.explanation: Delayed effects hide their source, so the link is plausible but not certain. The point is to ask, not to assume either answer.
items.reference:
Close-out versus calendar resumes
No close-out: fast layer recovers, slow layer waits
Later: a scramble, silence or resignation, looking unrelated
Close-out: named debrief plus a scheduled lighter stretch
Why: unpaid cost does not vanish; it reappears later without a visible link back.
items.learnMore:
Costumes for the same cost

The same unrepaired period can surface as a conflict, a scramble or a departure. Naming the period is what lets anyone connect them.

Common mistake

Solving each symptom locally and never asking what they share.

Symptoms only occur in the first week after a crunch

items.explanation: Passive-aggressive reviews, scrambles and resignations each have a local story, so the shared root goes unnamed.

items.prompt: Which of these is something a crunch spends?
choices: Office furniture
The company logo
Schedule slack
items.explanation: Slack borrowed to survive is not automatically returned.

items.prompt: How is borrowed schedule slack repaired?
choices: A lighter stretch with items removed
Telling the whole team to go easy for now
Adding a new weekly meeting
items.explanation: Only a real reduction in committed work restores slack.

items.prompt: What repairs trust between teammates after pressured calls?
choices: A group email thanking everyone involved
A direct talk, then follow-through
Waiting for time to pass
items.explanation: Trust needs a conversation and consistent behavior.

items.prompt: Why is 'morale' too vague to act on?
choices: It is always a perfectly accurate term
It can only be measured by HR
It does not say which thing was spent
items.explanation: Each spent thing needs its own repair.

items.prompt: What restores belief that urgent means something?
choices: Next requests handled at normal urgency
A reminder email defining what urgent means
Another round of crunch work
items.explanation: Behavior over the next few requests rebuilds the meaning.

items.prompt: Which spent item resolves on its own in days?
choices: Trust
Sleep
Schedule slack
items.explanation: Rest is passive; the others need active repair.

items.prompt: Which repair is just someone saying something out loud?
choices: Descoping two committed items
Handling urgent requests normally
Acknowledging the period was hard
items.explanation: Naming the difficulty costs nothing but is often skipped.

items.prompt: A PM mislabels a request as urgent mid-crunch. What does that spend?
choices: Belief in the urgent label
The team's supply of sleep
The sprint's committed slack
items.explanation: Crying wolf teaches people to discount the label.

items.prompt: After a crunch, the team is rested but starts ignoring urgent requests. Which spent item is the best explanation?
choices: Sleep, since rested people routinely ignore requests
Schedule slack, since slack governs how fast requests arrive
Trust in the system, since ignoring requests is a form of testing it
Belief that urgent means something, eroded when all was urgent
items.explanation: When everything was labeled urgent, the label stopped carrying information, and rested people still ignore a label they stopped believing.

sleep: rest, days
trust: a talk, then follow-through
slack: lighter stretch, items removed

Naming what was spent

Splitting a vague loss into specific items is what turns a feeling into a plan. Each item points to a different action.

Common mistake

Treating all of it as morale and offering one general kindness.

items.prompt: What is a crunch debrief about?
choices: The team's cost of getting through it
Which service failed during the outage itself
The next quarter's budget plan
items.explanation: A postmortem covers the system; a debrief covers the people.

items.prompt: What is step 1 of the debrief?
choices: Assign an owner to each bug
Name the hard period out loud
Schedule the next crunch for the quarter
items.explanation: Saying it plainly is the most-skipped step.

items.prompt: Which is a specific way to name it?
choices: Things were a bit busy lately
It has been quite a stretch
Four incidents in three weeks, paged nightly
items.explanation: Specific numbers show you actually noticed.

items.prompt: What does step 2 ask?
choices: What got spent, specifically
Who should be blamed first
How many tickets were closed
items.explanation: It looks for unease, skipped things and open decisions.

items.prompt: Which is a real rebuilding plan?
choices: We will try our best to take things easy
A lighter sprint ending on a named date
Everyone should rest when they can
items.explanation: Concrete items and an end date can be checked.

items.prompt: Why does step 4 exist?
choices: The first meeting always turns out a failure
Managers need practice at meetings
Rebuilding takes weeks, not one meeting
items.explanation: A single debrief starts repair but does not finish it.

items.prompt: What does an incident postmortem answer?
choices: What broke and what changes technically
What the crunch cost the people involved
Whether the team trusts each other
items.explanation: It is about the system, not the people.

items.prompt: Is one debrief enough?
choices: Yes, if it lasts a full hour or more
No, a check-back later is needed
Yes, if the whole team attends
items.explanation: One meeting starts the process only.

items.prompt: A manager's debrief covers outage causes and ends with 'thank you all'. Which framework step is most clearly missing?
choices: Asking what got spent, then a scheduled rebuilding plan
Naming that the period was hard, which thanks already covers
Checking back, which only matters for large teams
Assigning blame, which is needed for accountability
items.explanation: Thanks and a technical review do not ask the team's cost or schedule repair. Naming is partly covered; the plan is what is absent.
items.reference:
Four-step debrief
1. Name it, specifically, out loud
2. Ask what got spent
3. Concrete, scheduled rebuilding plan
4. Check back more than once
Why: each step closes a gap a vague 'good work, everyone' leaves open.
items.learnMore:
Debrief versus postmortem

A postmortem changes the system. A debrief changes the plan for the people. Skipping the second leaves the slow layer to chance.

Common mistake

Letting a filed postmortem stand in for the human conversation.
items.reflection: After a hard project you were part of, who asked what it cost you, if anyone? What would a useful version of that question have been?

A plan to revisit workload at the next quarterly review meeting
Two items removed, with normal pace resuming on a stated date
items.explanation: Only concrete items and a date can be verified later. The other options cannot be checked, so they cannot be enforced.
